title: Influence of Transcranial Electrical Stimulation on Arm and Hand Function After Cervical Spinal Cord Injury
official: Enhancing Motor Learning With Transcranial Electrical Stimulation for Upper Extremity Functional Restoration in People With Cervical Spinal Cord Injury
summary:
The goal of this pilot study is to find out how four different types of transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) affect brain activity, the process of acquiring new skills (also called motor learning), and hand function after cervical spinal cord injury (cSCI).

Participants will complete 5 study sessions: one sign-up session and four testing \& intervention sessions. Total participation will take about 18 hours. During the sign-up session, researchers will: discuss study details, review the participant's health history to make sure that it is safe for them to participate, perform tests to ensure that the participant meets the study criteria, and collect the participant's demographic information. During each testing \& intervention session, the participant will receive a different type of tES. Before and after getting tES, they will take part in tests that measure their brain activity and the strength, sensation, and function of their right hand.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* cervical spinal cord injury (neurological level C1-C8) that occurred at least one year ago
* International Standards for Neurological Classification of SCI/ASIA Impairment Scale (ISNCSCI/AIS) severity classification C or D
* self-reported limitations in right hand function
* volitional muscle activity in the right hand, as determined by a score ≥ 2 in at least one intrinsic hand muscle group evaluated in the Graded Redefined Assessment of Strength Sensibility and Prehension version 2 (GRASSP v2) strength subtest
* ability to follow instructions
* ability to communicate pain or discomfort
* ability and willingness to consent to participate in the study and authorize use of protected health information

Exclusion Criteria:

* spinal cord issues that are getting worse, such as degenerative or progressive vascular disorders of the spinal and/or spinal cord
* metal implant in the head
* history of uncontrolled seizures
* history of frequent or severe headaches
* damage to the nerves of the right arm/hand (lower motor neuron damage) as documented in the medical record, per participant report, or during in-person screening
* prior tendon or nerve transfer surgery in the right arm/hand
* severe pain, hypersensitivity, or contractures of the right arm/hand that would limit participation in arm and hand training
* broken skin or wounds on your head/scalp where stimulation will be applied
* if you're a woman, and you are pregnant, think you might be, or are actively trying to become pregnant
* you have any other health issue that the lead investigators think could make it unsafe for you to join the study
